summary: This document lets networks with IPv4-only legacy clients use DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 in a Relay Agent. RFC 7341 covers only the client, and this builds on it.

plainLanguage.summary: Old IPv4 devices can still get their settings in an IPv6 network, with a go-between helping.

questions: ipv4 clients ipv6 only network dhcp
how do ipv4 only clients use dhcpv6
subtitle: Lets a relay in the network do the DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 work for IPv4-only clients that cannot do it themselves.

tldr.problem: RFC 7341 carries DHCPv4 messages over DHCPv6, but it needs support in the client. Legacy IPv4-only hosts cannot be updated, so they cannot use it.
tldr.mechanism: A Relay Agent (the 4o6RA) acts as the DHCP 4o6 client. It wraps the legacy client's DHCPv4 request in a DHCPV4-QUERY and unwraps the DHCPV4-RESPONSE for the client.
tldr.outcome: Legacy hosts can get IPv4 configuration from a DHCPv6 server with no change to the host. Topology information is lost unless the 4o6RA is paired with a Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent.

today: RFC 9928 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026. It is not obsoleted or updated by any later RFC, and it extends the use of RFC 7341 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: The Problem with Legacy IPv4 Clients
sections.content:
RFC 7341 describes how DHCPv4 messages can be carried inside DHCPv6, so IPv4 addresses and other DHCPv4 settings can be provisioned across IPv6-only networks. Deploying it requires support in the DHCP client and at the DHCPv6 server.

That fails when the client sits in a host that only supports IPv4 and cannot easily be replaced or updated. The DHCPv6 Relay Agent specification in RFC 9915, together with the Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (RFC 6221), has no way to handle legacy DHCPv4 either, short of requiring the client to do the encapsulation.

This document needs no new protocol or extension. It defines a new use case for RFC 7341: a Relay Agent in an intermediate node such as a switch or router does the encapsulation and decapsulation instead of the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Old devices cannot learn the new way of asking for an address. So a helper in the middle learns it for them.

sections.title: Applicability Scope
sections.content:
The mechanism applies to the configuration phase of hosts that need an IPv4 address when a DHCPv4 server is not reachable directly. The host cannot implement a DHCP client conformant to RFC 7341 because it is connected to an IPv4-only network. A DHCPv6 server that can provide IPv4 addresses by the mechanisms of RFC 7341 does exist.

The document also defines terms. A 4o6RA is a Relay Agent that implements the DHCP 4o6 transport as specified here. A Layer 3 Relay Agent (L3RA) is a DHCP Relay Agent per RFC 9915 that is not a Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA).
sections.plainLanguage: It is for the case where the device is stuck on an old kind of network but a newer kind of server is the one that can help.

sections.title: How the 4o6 Relay Agent Works
sections.content:
The legacy DHCPv4 client is on a Layer 2 network. The 4o6RA sits between it and an IPv6 network that holds the DHCP 4o6 server. The legacy client is not aware that it is being served via a DHCP 4o6 service.

The 4o6RA takes the client's role as defined in RFC 7341. It picks a suitable interface to act as a DHCPv6 client, finds a suitable DHCPv6 server or Relay Agent and gets the IPv6 configuration it needs. It must request the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option with an Option Request option before it can use the transport. All client prerequisites in Section 5 of RFC 7341 apply to it.

The message format is unchanged from RFC 9915, to stay interoperable with existing relays and servers. The 4o6RA creates the DHCPV4-QUERY message and encapsulates the DHCP request it received from the legacy client.

When a DHCPV4-RESPONSE arrives, the 4o6RA looks for the DHCPv4 message option. If it is missing or the message is not well-formed, the message MUST be discarded. Otherwise the 4o6RA MUST extract the DHCPv4 message and forward it to the requesting client, provided it is correct and can actually be forwarded.

Layer 2 Relay Agents that receive these messages handle them as in Section 6 of RFC 6221. DHCPv6 servers are expected to comply with RFC 7341, and this document adds no requirements for them. Intermediate relays behave according to Section 10 of RFC 7341.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper takes the old device's note, puts it in a new envelope, and sends it off. When the answer comes back, it takes the answer out of the envelope and hands it over.

sections.title: Topology Discovery and the LDRA
sections.content:
Networks sometimes configure a host based on where it is attached. DHCP relays supply that topology information (see RFC 7969). In IPv4, only the first Relay Agent SHOULD set the giaddr field, so only part of the topology is carried. In DHCPv6, all Relay Agents SHOULD send link-address and Interface-ID options describing the complete path to the server.

Putting 4o6 at the edge hides the Layer 2 network from the DHCPv6 relays behind it, because a 4o6RA alone puts no interface information in the encapsulated message. That breaks topology propagation.

To keep it, the document RECOMMENDS combining any 4o6RA implementation with an LDRA in a back-to-back structure. The LDRA must have a way to get interface information so it can supply the Interface-ID option on outgoing DHCPV4-QUERY messages, as in Section 5.3.2 of RFC 6221. How the two exchange that information is out of scope.

If the same node hosts the 4o6RA and the DHCP 4o6 server, the 4o6RA alone may be enough.
sections.plainLanguage: If the helper does not say which door the note came through, the server cannot tell where the device lives. So the helper is paired with another helper who writes that down.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Clients do not know a 4o6RA exists, so the network must steer all DHCPv4 broadcast and unicast messages to and from clients through a 4o6RA.

The text offers two ways. One is to place the 4o6RA centrally, where it can intercept all client traffic. The other is to use Network Address Translation (NAT) with the 4o6RA address for unicast messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Every letter the old device sends has to go past the helper, or the helper cannot do the job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7341 still apply. Since the legacy client does not know about the encapsulation, the 4o6RA has to provide the protections in Section 12 of RFC 7341.

Unlike RFC 7341, here the client sends and receives DHCPv4 messages. In a badly configured network, where a client shares a Layer 2 scope with a DHCPv4 server, messages could reach that server without passing the 4o6RA. This can cause erroneous state and misconfigurations that affect reachability, but the document calls it a deployment error rather than a security concern. Attacks from inside the network are not a new concern introduced here.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old device can also reach a different server by accident, things can get mixed up. That is a setup mistake, not a new danger.

sections.title: Example: Radio Units in a 3GPP RAN
sections.content:
Appendix A gives a use case. In a 3GPP Radio Access Network, Baseband Units (BBUs) configure Radio Units (RUs) according to the cell and sector each RU serves, which depends on cabling. When BBUs and RUs are connected through a Layer 2 switched network, the BBU needs topology knowledge to configure each RU properly.

If RUs are IPv4-only and cannot implement a DHCP 4o6 client, the topology discovery mechanisms of Section 3.2 of RFC 7969 can still be used by putting a 4o6RA in the switches, as this document describes.
sections.plainLanguage: Many antenna boxes must be set up differently depending on which cable they use. The helper in the switch tells the server which cable each box is on.
